paragraphs.title: Cursing the Day and Night of Birth

easy.explanation: Job opened his speech by cursing the day of his birth.
easy.q: What did Job curse at the beginning of his speech?

answers: That it would become a feast
easy.explanation: Job asked that the day be darkness.
easy.q: What did Job ask to happen to that day?

easy.explanation: Job also cursed the night in which it was said that a man child was conceived.
easy.q: What other time did Job curse?

answers: That it would be removed from the calendar
medium.explanation: He wished that the night would not be joined to the days of the year or counted among the months.
medium.q: What did Job want to happen to the night of his conception?

answers: That it would be full of joy
That it would be alone and desolate
That it would be very bright
medium.explanation: Job wanted the night to have no joyful voice within it.
medium.q: What does Job mean by asking that the night be “solitary”?

answers: Darkness and the removal of light
medium.explanation: Job repeatedly calls for darkness, fear, and the absence of light.
medium.q: What do most of Job’s requests in this passage seek?

answers: He curses both his birth and his conception
He wants the day to be longer
challenge.explanation: The day represents his birth, while the night represents his conception.
challenge.q: Why does Job speak of both the day and the night?

answers: A desire to remove all joy from it
A desire for people to remain awake
challenge.explanation: Job wishes the night to be empty of joy and celebration.
challenge.q: What does the request that no joyful voice enter the night express?

answers: It expands from the day to darkness, erasure, and judgment against the night
It moves from private joy to public joy
It changes from the night to a description of his wealth
challenge.explanation: The curse grows from the day of his birth to the night of conception and the removal of light.
challenge.q: How does Job’s curse intensify through the passage?

paragraphs.title: The Wish Never to Have Been Born

answers: Why he did not die from the womb
Why he was not made a king
Why he did not see the night
easy.explanation: Job asks why he did not die from the womb.
easy.q: What does Job ask about the time before his birth?

answers: Why the knees received him and the breasts nourished him
Why he was sent on a journey
easy.explanation: He asks why the knees prevented him and why the breasts gave him suck.
easy.q: What does Job ask about the care he received as an infant?

answers: An hidden untimely birth or an infant that never saw light
easy.explanation: Job says he might have been hidden as an untimely birth or an infant that never saw light.
easy.q: How does Job describe what he might have been if he had not lived?

answers: Both express his wish not to continue living
Both show that he wanted to see the light
medium.explanation: Job regrets that he did not die in the womb or immediately after birth.
medium.q: How are Job’s questions about the womb and birth related?

answers: They recall the care and nourishment he received
medium.explanation: The knees and breasts represent the care and nourishment given to a newborn child.
medium.q: Why do the knees and breasts strengthen Job’s lament?

answers: A child who did not live or see the light
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to a child hidden from the world and unable to see its light.
medium.q: What does “an hidden untimely birth” mean in this passage?

answers: The wish to remain hidden and never enter the world
The wish to return to wealth
challenge.explanation: Both images express Job’s desire not to be born or see the world’s light.
challenge.q: What idea is expressed by the comparison between an hidden birth and infants that never saw light?

answers: He asks why he did not die before or immediately after birth
He asks for more care and nourishment
challenge.explanation: Job presents birth and life as things he would rather not have experienced.
challenge.q: How do Job’s questions show that he regrets his birth?

answers: Being hidden in darkness versus seeing the light of the world
challenge.explanation: Job wishes to have been hidden rather than brought into the light of the world.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in this passage?

easy.explanation: Job says that there the wicked cease from troubling.
easy.q: What do the wicked cease from in the place Job describes?

easy.explanation: Job describes the weary as being at rest there.

answers: He is free from his master
easy.explanation: Job says that the servant is free from his master.
easy.q: What happens to the servant there?

answers: The small and great, servant and master
medium.explanation: The passage says, “The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master.”
medium.q: Which different groups are described as being together there?

answers: Both express release from suffering and social control
medium.explanation: The passage presents the grave as a place of rest and freedom from oppression.
medium.q: What do the rest of the weary and the freedom of servants have in common?

answers: The voice of one who presses or burdens others
medium.explanation: The prisoners no longer hear the voice of the person who oppresses them.
medium.q: What does “the voice of the oppressor” refer to?

answers: It is a place of rest and equality
It is a place of competition
It is a place of wealth
challenge.explanation: Job describes it as a place of rest, calm, and release from social distinctions.
challenge.q: What central idea comes from Job’s description of the grave?

answers: It shows that earthly control does not exist there
It shows that the servant becomes the master
It shows that the master becomes richer
challenge.explanation: The servant is free from his master, showing that the usual relationship of power has ended.
challenge.q: Why is the servant and master comparison important?

answers: The prisoners are at rest and hear no oppressor
challenge.explanation: Their silence and calm emphasize the end of pressure and forced labor.
challenge.q: How does the statement about prisoners support the idea of rest?

paragraphs.title: The Question of Suffering and Longing for Death

answers: Why the suffering person is given life and light
easy.explanation: Job asks why light and life are given to a person in misery.
easy.q: Why does Job ask, “Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery”?

easy.explanation: They long for death, but it does not come.
easy.q: What do the people in these verses long for?

answers: When they can find the grave
easy.explanation: Job says they rejoice when they can find the grave.

answers: They do not see life’s light as a blessing but as a burden
medium.explanation: Job describes people in bitterness who long for death rather than continued life.
medium.q: What contrast appears between the light of life and the desire of the sufferers?

answers: His path is clear to everyone
His path is hidden and he cannot find direction
medium.explanation: Job describes a person whose way is hidden and whom God has hedged in.
medium.q: What does “whose way is hid” mean?

answers: The grave is seen as an answer to the longing for death
The grave represents success in life
The grave represents a return to work
medium.explanation: The sufferers rejoice at finding a grave because they desire death.
medium.q: What is the relationship between seeking a grave and rejoicing?

answers: It asks why the life of one who suffers greatly continues
It asks how to lengthen the day
It asks why the stars shine
challenge.explanation: Job is questioning not merely light itself but the continuation of life amid intense suffering.
challenge.q: Why is “Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery?” a question about the meaning of life?

answers: Death is viewed as more desirable than continued life
The sufferer wants to return to the world
The sufferer is looking for a home
challenge.explanation: Joy at finding a grave shows how deeply the person longs for death.
challenge.q: What does rejoicing at finding a grave reveal about the strength of the suffering?

answers: Both express confusion and a sense of restriction
challenge.explanation: The hidden path and the hedge suggest that the sufferer feels without direction and unable to move forward.
challenge.q: How does the hidden way relate to being hedged in by God?

paragraphs.title: Fear Fulfilled and the Absence of Rest

easy.explanation: Job says, “For my sighing cometh before I eat.”
easy.q: What comes before Job eats his food?

easy.explanation: Job says that what he greatly feared had come upon him.
easy.q: What happened to the things Job greatly feared?

easy.explanation: Job says he was not in safety, had no rest, and was not quiet.

medium.explanation: Job compares his loud cries to waters being poured out.
medium.q: What does “my roarings” mean in this passage?

answers: They show suffering that continues without relief
medium.explanation: His sighing and cries show that suffering overwhelms him continually.
medium.q: How are Job’s sighing and roarings related to his lack of rest?

medium.explanation: The passage ends by saying that trouble came upon him.
medium.q: What came to Job instead of safety, rest, and quiet?

answers: His suffering came before even ordinary daily needs
challenge.explanation: The sighing came before eating, showing that suffering dominated even his daily routine.
challenge.q: What does the fact that sighing came before eating emphasize?

answers: The fears he dreaded came upon him and brought trouble
The trouble made him forget his fears
challenge.explanation: Job says that what he feared came to him, and trouble followed instead of quiet.
challenge.q: How are fear and trouble connected at the end of the passage?

answers: Job cannot find safety, quiet, or rest because suffering overwhelms him
Job describes his success in life
challenge.explanation: The verses conclude with Job’s statement that he has no rest or quiet because trouble has come.
challenge.q: What is the concluding idea of the passage?
